name: The Veil of Ignorance
statement: Choose the rules of society without knowing which person in it you will be.
statementAccent: which person in it you will be
meaning: The veil of ignorance is John Rawls's method for choosing fair principles of justice. Imagine selecting the rules for society from behind a veil that hides your own place in it — your class, race, sex, talents, wealth, and even your idea of the good life. Not knowing which position you will occupy, and unable to rig the rules in your own favour, you will choose principles that are fair to everyone. The device is the defining feature of what Rawls calls the original position, his reworking of the social contract.
mechanism: The veil enforces impartiality by stripping the chooser of the self-knowledge that would let them tilt the rules toward their own advantage. Parties retain general knowledge — of economics, psychology, and how societies work — but not their particular identity, so any principle they favour must be acceptable whatever position they turn out to hold. Rawls argues this leads to reasoning by maximin, maximising the minimum: since the choice fixes your whole life and there is no basis for gambling on probabilities, you secure the best worst-case rather than chase a higher average, and so you guard the least advantaged.

examples.text: Behind the veil, Rawls argues, parties choose equal basic liberties for all, and then the difference principle: inequalities are allowed only if they benefit the least advantaged.
The everyday analogue: whoever cuts the cake takes the last slice, so not knowing which piece is yours makes you divide it evenly — impartiality enforced by ignorance of your position.

Economist John Harsanyi reached the opposite conclusion from a similar device: assigning equal probability to each position, a rational chooser would maximise average utility, not protect the worst-off.

variants.name: Harsanyi's earlier version
variants.text: Harsanyi developed the same choose-behind-a-veil reasoning about fifteen years before Rawls but derived utilitarianism, showing the device alone does not settle the outcome.

variants.name: The communitarian critique
variants.text: Michael Sandel's objection that the party behind the veil is an 'unencumbered self', stripped of the attachments and ends that actually make deliberation about the good possible.

whyItMatters: It is foundational to modern liberal political philosophy. Rawls's 'A Theory of Justice' revived normative political theory in the English-speaking world and made the veil of ignorance a central tool for reasoning about fairness, distribution, and the legitimacy of institutions. The device has spread well beyond philosophy — into welfare economics, law, and recent debates over fairness in algorithms — as a portable test for impartiality: would you accept this rule not knowing where in the system you would land?

working.text: reason about a rule by imagining you do not know which affected party you will be, so you cannot tailor it to your advantage.
retain facts about how societies and people work while hiding your particular identity, which is what makes the choice both informed and impartial.
test principles by how they treat the least advantaged position, since behind the veil that position could be yours.

limits: It is a normative thought experiment and method, not an empirical law, and its conclusions depend on contested assumptions rather than following from the setup alone. Harsanyi derived utilitarianism from a similar veil, so the device does not by itself yield Rawls's egalitarian principles; the maximin result rests on disputed premises about risk aversion and choice under uncertainty. Critics from Nozick's libertarianism to Sandel's communitarianism to feminist and Senian objections challenge both the method and its output. The setup is canonical, but its specific two-principles-and-maximin conclusion is one much-debated interpretation.
misreadings: It is not a description of how societies actually formed — it is an explicitly hypothetical device of representation, not a historical contract. Behind the veil you do not know nothing: parties keep general knowledge and lose only their particular identity and circumstances. And the veil does not by itself entail Rawls's difference principle; Harsanyi's utilitarian derivation from the same idea shows the egalitarian conclusion depends on Rawls's further, contested assumptions.
origin: Introduced by John Rawls in 'A Theory of Justice' (1971) as the core of the original position, within the social-contract tradition of Locke, Rousseau, and Kant; a closely related device was used earlier by the economist John Harsanyi in the 1950s to argue for utilitarianism.
